Mr. Speaker, I have the honour and the privilege under Standing Order 36 to present a petition signed by a number of grain and oilseed producers in Canada who are experiencing severe shortages of cash flow because of the present prices for agricultural commodities.
Your petitioners ask this House to convince the government to provide immediate assistance for these cash-strapped farmers.

speakeroldname: Mr. Brian L. Gardiner (Prince George -Bulkley Valley):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have the pleasure and the duty to present a petition to the House today. It is a very important petition. It is signed by residents primarily from the central interior of British Columbia and it is
regarding water diversion projects. They call upon Parliament to urge the government to state categorically that it will not permit our freshwater rivers to be dammed and diverted into the U.S.A. and to state that our Canadian rivers are not for sale.

Mr. Speaker, I have the honour to present a petition from people in Malartic, La Motte, Saint-Mathieu, Riviere-Heva, Cadillac and Dubuisson in Abitibi who say that preventive withdrawal for pregnant women is a necessary and desirable option for working women.
For these reasons, they ask Parliament, when it reviews the Canada Labour Code, to consider seriously the deficiencies in it and to recognize the need to include in the Code clauses concerning preventive withdrawal for pregnant women, with pay.

Mr. Speaker, it is my pleasure today to rise and present a petition signed by many Canadian farmers. They state that grain and oilseed producers are experiencing the most severe shortage of cash flow in the history of the industry.
They call on the Government of Canada and they humbly pray that it will see fit to provide more assistance to them in their severe problems.

Mr. Speaker, once again I am honoured to rise in the House pursuant to Standing Order 36 and present a petition on behalf of farmers from western Ontario. They state that the Government of Canada has failed to provide sufficient cash flow assistance to farmers during the transition from the old ad hoc programs to the new safety net programs in order that farmers may meet their financial obligations and preserve the family farm. The undersigned petitioners humbly pray and call upon Parliament to urge the government to provide such assistance as proposed by

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 42A.
That Bill C-4 be amended in Clause 319 by striking out line 41 at
page 162 and substituting the following therefor:
"ling annual meeting, appoint two auditors, who shall be independent of each other, to".

He said: Mr. Speaker, the purpose of this amendment is to require that financial institutions appoint two auditors rather than a single auditor.
Government Orders
At present the Bank Act requires two auditors. Other financial institutions have one auditor. It was amazing that while we were in committee the government and the Official Opposition even changed the requirement of two auditors for a bank to one auditor for a bank. The banks wanted to have two auditors. I think it is safe to say that. They wanted that extended to some of these other financial institutions. In fact now more than ever, when all of these changes are completed, we have all of this commingling, this intermingling where banks can own trust companies, where banks can own insurance companies, insurance companies can own trust companies. When you have all of this,-
Cannibalism.

-this cannibalism, and that is a good word to describe it, when we have had all of this feeding frenzy, the situation will become even more complex. I am afraid, as much as I have a lot of faith in the regulatory agency, OSFI, I want to say that OSFI is incapable of doing an audit on these.
OSFI depends on the auditors' reports. In 1980, the Economic Council of Canada found that there were external and internal factors for the failures. The dominant ones were the internal factors. These all have to do with questionable loan practices. Questionable practices were also discovered whereby managers attempted to secure gains for themselves at the expense of depositors and investors.
OSFI depends on these internal and external auditor's reports. I want to quote Michael Mackenzie's evidence before the committee when we were looking at Standard Trust. Michael Mackenzie is the Superintendent of Financial Institutions.
Mr. Mackenzie said, and I quote him, and this was in his evidence before the Standing Committee on Finance on June 13, 1991:
We said we relied on these financial statements that you audit as primary evidence of the financial soundness of the company. In that context, if there are conditions or transactions that you know will effectively threaten the solvency of the company, your duty is to tell the management and tell us at the same time. If you see transactions that are beyond the powers of the company, you are to do the same.
Then we went on to state that we wanted to review their working papers so we established a framework of reliance here that did not exist before. To me in this case we had put the auditors on notice. We relied on them to do the loan examination at that time. If for example there were these undue loan concentrations and so forth, there is a sense in which if they are infracting the Ontario or the federal act's lines or

November 26, 1991
Government Orders
rules on asset concentrations, we would have expected them to report
to management and to report to us at the same time.
The point I am trying to make there and that Mr. Mackenzie makes is that it shows how dependent OSFI is on the auditors' reports.
OSFI does not do on sight auditing of all the financial institutions in the country. They depend on these reports.
When the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants came before us, it recommended two auditors. We support the audit appointment provisions for banks set out in Bill C-19 which (a) provide for dual auditors to be appointed for large banks, (b) provide for a minimum threshold to determine which banks must appoint dual auditors and (c) do not require banks to rotate auditors.
They go on to point out in the brief that major banks are an essential part of the Canadian economy and it is essential to maintain widespread confidence in the economy.
The banking industry is highly concentrated. A few very large institutions account for a very large part of commercial lending. The effectiveness of the auditing system is therefore particularly important to the positive confidence upon which the the continued functioning of Canadian capital markets ultimately rests. A reservation in the auditor's report, whereby a disagreement with the bank would be made public, could damage the confidence of depositors and in extreme cases could cause a run on the banks. Auditors may therefore be perceived as extremely hesitant to express a reservation of opinion.
The importance of auditors at the present moment in a highly concentrated banking system is ultimately important. Imagine how much more concentrated it is going to get when all of these bills get passed. Already you see the urge to merge. You see trust companies looking for partners. Insurance companies are buying out trust companies.
It seems to me that there is a need to protect the interests of the depositors and dual auditors is a requirement.
We all remember the collapse of the CCB and the Northland Bank. At that time the Hon. Willard S. Estey was appointed commissioner to look into the failure of those two banks. His recommendation No. 20 is particularly important. This is what Justice Estey recommended.
It is recommended that no change be made to the dual auditor
system as provided by Section 2(37) of the Bank Act.
We have ample evidence that the two auditor system provides safety and assurance to depositors. What did the Liberals and the Conservatives do in the committee? Not only did they increase the amount of external auditing in the financial institutions, they simply said to the banks: "You do not have to give two auditor reports anymore, only one." They wish to reduce the auditors to one. I cannot understand it. I find it very very incomprehensible that these bills are going to allow a complete restructuring of financial institutions.
I suggest that we are not going to have myriads of financial institutions across the country anymore. We will have a smaller number of very large banks, financial institutions, whose primary aim is to compete globally. That is all I hear from the Conservatives in the government. "We have to be global competitors." Now I am starting to hear it from the Liberals who since last weekend have discovered global competition.
That is where Bills C-4, C-19, C-28 and C-34 are taking financial institution structure in this country. They are reducing financial institutions to a veiy small number where competition will not be introverted but extroverted. In other words, we are going to have to depend on the American Expresses of this world to provide Canadians at home with the competition. We are going to depend on financial institutions outside of Canada to come in here and provide the competition. The competition will not be generated from within the country.
In the midst of this we have had problems with financial institutions such as Standard Trust and Principal Trust which I understand were in the provincial jurisdiction. It cost the Canada Deposit Insurance, which is the Canadian taxpayer, some $200 million to $300 million to bail out Standard Trust depositors. We keep picking up the pieces.
November 26, 1991

There is no doubt that the amount of money which has come out of taxpayers' pockets to support the deposit insurance for trust companies and banks that have failed is about equal between banks and trust and loan companies. In the last dozen years there have been only a couple of large banks in the west that have failed. What we paid out through the deposit insurance for those two banks was equalled by all the trust and loans companies that have gone under.
Since the regulator depends on the audits of financial institutions, it does not seem fair to depositors and the taxpayers of Canada that this is the time to be easing up on the brake. It seems to me the argument I am making is for more scrutiny, not less scrutiny. That is one of the ways that we have been able to keep confidence in the system.
I am prepared to state, because I have stated it previously many times, the Canadian banking system has a lot of integrity in Canada and in the world. The Canadian banks that have been developed with the regulatory systems we have in place are some of the safest financial institutions in the world.
If we look at the Japanese banks, the German banks and the American banks, for God's sake, Canadian banks are far superior. We have been able to regulate them and because we have had the brakes on, they have been able to develop and grow.
The member for Mississauga South should take cognizance of this amendment and reverse the mistake he made in the committee of reducing dual auditors in banks to one. Let us extend the dual auditor system to the financial institutions across the country.

Mr. Speaker, I want to thank the hon. member for Nickel Belt for his concern. There is no question that the system depends on auditors, it depends on actuaries and it depends on top quality reporting. That is the reason this bill and the other bills that will follow deal very extensively with the duties of auditors, the requirement to report, the requirement to certify and all of those requirements that are there.
The question is: Would two be better than one?
I have the advantage of having been around this matter for a long time. In the spring of 1985 the finance committee conducted a major study into the problems of
Government Orders
the refinancing of the Canadian Commercial Bank. I remember very clearly a situation where we had a representative from the Clarkson company and a representative from Peat Marwick and company before us. When we got into the issue of what happened, one auditor looked at the other and said: "Well, Alphonse, weren't you going to do that?" The other one said: "That was your responsibility".
This business of having two auditors and saying two is better than one is like saying that two drivers to steer a car is better than one. It is such nonsense. The fact is that we need to have one person responsible as the auditor, one firm responsible. Let us make sure that firm has responsibilities, let us make sure that firm does its work right, but let us not try to say that if you have two you are going to be better off. As a practical matter, you are not.
What we have right now is a rotating system where an auditing firm, under the banks anyway, works for a veiy short period of time, a year, and then is off the case. The problem is that it takes a length of time for a firm to really get a grip on the intricacies of the internal accounting system.
It is my view and the view of the government that we have been allowing things to slip for too long by pretending to rely on two auditors when in fact there is very little protection that way at all. Indeed, you really need to have one who is responsible and you have to make sure that you can pin the responsibility on that one firm.
The arbitrage that goes on right now where there are situations of two auditors is not acceptable.
I understand some members of the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants would like us to expand then-work. I understand things are tough today out in the field and the more work you can get the better and the more retainers you can get the better and that would be fine. I suppose that is a good way of feather-bedding, if you want to put it that way.
I am surprised at my friend from Nickel Belt wanting to sponsor that feather-bedding. I am surprised he does not realize just how much better off we are with one auditor than two. That is the reason why the finance committee suggested for Bill C-19, which will follow, the one auditor and that is, of course, the reason why we

Government Orders
ought to remain in the one-auditor context in terms of trust companies and insurance companies.
May I point out that we have operated well with one auditor. Canada Trust is certainly larger than some of our banks, perhaps larger than the Canadian National Bank. I must say that there is no real merit in saying one will not do because one does well and does very well and that is the way we ought to keep it. We ought to keep the situation where we have one auditor responsible, one auditor subject to the very detailed requirements that this bill and the companion bills require and impose upon that auditing firm.
While we believe that we ought to follow through with the Canadian Institute of Chartered Accountants handbook as a method of standard, we believe that standard is best enforced when you make one person, one firm, responsible for the work. When you have one person responsible then you know where to put the blame if there is a problem. When you wind up with that problem defused it is after you, Alphonse, and we have had enough of after you, Alphonses.

Mr. Speaker, amendment 42A. which states that trust companies should have two auditors was actually discussed in the finance committee. This amendment that we have before us this morning actually contradicts the decision that was made in the finance committee which would allow a trust company to choose whether it needed one auditor or two.
Under the existing legislation, trust companies have one auditor. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions and the finance committee, as I mentioned a minute ago, felt that there was no obvious reason why we should require trust companies to have two auditors. In fact, as the hon. member for Mississauga has stated, and it was also indicated in the finance committee, there is a possibility if you have two that one auditor could believe that the other auditor was doing something that he is not and things could get missed. The hon. member for Nickel Belt mentioned the Estey inquiry which looked into the failure of the Canadian Bank and the Northland Bank. I want to remind him that Mr. Estey stated in that inquiry that the auditor system of having two auditors would not have made any difference at all to these two banks. Why would chartered banks want to have two auditors. That makes work. We also have to remember that auditors cost money and really, who is going to end
up paying the price tag? It is the customer or the trust company.
If I felt that it was absolutely necessary that a trust company should have two auditors, then certainly I would vote for this amendment. Obviously, from what we heard in the finance committee, and as I said, the Superintendent of Financial Institutions does not see any reason for this, I do not see any reason why we should inflict this cost on the Canadian public. If it is an unnecessary cost, why make the trust company customers pay for it?
I repeat, this was brought up in the finance committee. We voted against it. The Superintendent of Financial Institutions does not see any reason for it so, therefore, I will be voting against it.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 58.
That Bill C-4 be amended in Clause 416 by striking out line 31 at
page 214 and substituting the following therefor:
"(2) Except as permitted in the Act or the regulations, a company shall not act in Canada as".
November 26, 1991

Motion No. 60.
That Bill C-4 be amended in Clause 416 by adding immediately after line 42 at page 214 the following:
"(4) A company may, with the prior consent of a customer, provide an insurance company, agent or broker with information respecting the customer.
(5)	A consent given pursuant to subsection (4) shall be contained in a separate document that deals only with subject matter of the consent."

He said: Mr. Speaker, Motion No. 58 would allow the regulations to permit companies to engage in certain activities of an insurance agent or to provide space in a branch to a person engaged in the placing of insurance.
I want to just briefly repeat the position we have taken with respect to the whole deregulation of the financial institutions scene as envisaged in these bills.
We have said that insurance companies ought to do things that are related to insurance companies; banks, things that are related to banking; trust and loan companies, things that are of a fiduciary nature related to trust and loan companies. This is the position we have taken. We therefore have no objection to a bank marketing insurance through its branches. We have no problem with that, but we have real concerns. We oppose banks owning insurance companies because we see the breakdown of the system and a concentration of economic power in a few hands. That is a concern. The one fallout from that is the consumer. We have argued that banks ought to be allowed to market insurance through then-branches.
Many of the insurance companies which appeared before the finance committee said: "Oh, no, you cannot allow that at all. You cannot allow that because if you allow them to market insurance they are going to twist the arms of the consumer, they are going to tight sell, and a whole host of other nasty things". As it turns out many of those large insurance companies which came before the finance committee own financial institutions, trust companies, in Europe. Lo and behold, guess what they do in Europe? Those financial institutions that are owned by the insurance companies here in Canada market insurance through their branches. The question was put to them: Do those financial institutions that you own in Europe use all of these nasty practices: tight
Government Orders
selling, arm twisting, and a whole host of other things, to get the consumer to buy your insurance products? Of course not. They do not do it. They do not do it at all.
So they say.

Yes. We pointed out, Mr. Speaker, that in fact there is evidence, contrary to what the Liberal critic said yesterday, there were studies done in the United States which show in fact that this marketing of insurance through financial institution branches brings down the cost of insurance.
It was interesting after that that those hearings received publicity. I received a letter on April 24, 1991. The member from Mississauga South would be interested because this is a gentleman who has an insurance brokerage in Mississauga. He writes to me, "Dear Mr. Rodriguez", and he goes through the issues, and he says: "The comments about over-priced policies and dividends is a potshot of McLeod's at Mutual, which pays dividends on its policies". He is talking here about Professor McLeod, who appeared before the finance committee and was very critical of the insurance companies. "McLeod correctly points out that the dividends on return of an overpayment of premium and that is why they are not taxed.
Mutual Life is owned by the policyholders, not by shareholders. This means that for practical purposes management does not have to answer to anyone. For example, Mutual Life recently changed agents over to level commissions. They are to receive 20 per cent for life of new premium sales. Under the old system they received 80 per cent in year one, 20 per cent in year two and 5 per cent thereafter. The agents complained that the combination of the old renewals and the new level commissions would put them below a living income. Mutual solved the problem by agreeing to pay the new commission on the existing business too. This means the old business is being charged for commissions twice". Is that not marvellous? As a salesman I would love to get paid twice on my book of business. "However the owners of the insurance companies would object to cost". Mutual Life has no owners to complain.
Fourth, on the subject of competition, I enclose a partial listing of the companies in Canada. I assure the House that there are a fair number I had never heard of until I read this list. Many of these companies were created for specific limited purposes and not for general

November 26, 1991
Government Orders
sales to the public. Many are not active outside their province or head office.
There are, however, still lots of insurance companies available to the public. Unfortunately the public does not shop around for life insurance. If it did, as we can see by the survey there are some companies that should get very little business.
Members of the public do not shop around. They buy from the company agent who approaches them. The agents of the big companies that represent about 80 per cent of the market have contracts which specifically prohibit them from recommending the insurance of any company other than their own.
The banks would add a new level of competition in that they would write business for which they may have gone to a life company agent.
The lack of real competition, however, is contributable to the domination of the industry by the few large companies that field their own exclusive agents. While I have nothing against companies fielding exclusive agents, I do resent their success and stifling competition.
For example, in Ontario which is probably the largest market in Canada brokerage is specifically prohibited, that is in Ontario an agent is not allowed to represent more than one company except for the Insurance Act which he enclosed a copy of. He goes on to say that if the banks sell the companies they own not much would change in this picture. The clients still would not be shopping around and the seller would be selling for only one company. This may be what MacLeod was referring to when he said that he could see no advantage to the consumer of banks owning insurance companies.
He said: "Personally I think the public could only gain if the banks worked as agent brokers. They could then compete on insurance costs as they do on loan rates. Would this require a change in the provincial laws that prohibit or restrict brokerage? The public would benefit if there was a lot more activity pushing inexpensive term insurance. Bank clerks could be trained to sell a lot of this type of insurance. Canadians, in my opinion, are over premium and under-insured".
That is Jim Bulloch. He has an insurance brokerage in Mississauga. There is an informed opinion of what goes on in the industry. It is one that makes the argument for the banks to market insurance.
I was just reading an article in The Financial Post the other day that makes the same argument in a different way. It points out, for example, that Sun Life Assurance of Canada has integrated its Sun Life Trust branches with its insurance operations. This allows the insurance agents to provide trust services to clients and permits clients to buy GICs and arrange mortgages over the telephone.
That is one of the other arguments we heard, that bank clerks are not trained to sell insurance. We have a whole pile of insurance agents out there on the telephone and in person selling financial products. They sell RRSPs, annuities, GICs, and now they are selling mortgages over the telephone. What is the point? What is this argument for training?
We have taken this position that the banks ought to be able to market insurance through their branches. They should not be allowed to own the insurance companies.
Turning to my other motion, Motion No. 60, even if the government gets its way and separates the insurance operation from the bank operation and if the bank owns an insurance company and has a separate operation, it is forbidding the bank, even with the customer's approval, to send information to the insurance subsidiary of the bank. My Motion No. 60 says on matters relating to insurance that with the customer's signed approval that information ought to be passed on to the bank's subsidiary. It seems to me that makes some sense.
I go into a branch where I do all my banking and I want to get insurance. The bank manager says: "I am sorry, I cannot talk to you about that. You will have to go to the directory and see where our branch is located and go over there and talk to them". I have to go there and give them all the information that I have given to the bank with respect to the insurance purchase.
It seems to me that my amendment would give the right to the customer. The right rests with the customer. If the customer wants the information to be passed on to the bank's subsidiary for insurance then he ought to be able to sign that and that information ought to go over to the subsidiary. It seems to me that is even proposed by
November 26, 1991

the owner of one of the largest insurance companies. Power Corporation has recommended that and it owns Great West Life. It seems to me that it has also recommended that the customer should have the right to authorize the bank to send the information to the insurance subsidiary.

Mr. Speaker, it is the principle of the bill that insurance companies do insurance, trust companies do trust work, and banks do banking work. If trust companies want to be involved in insurance work they have to own an insurance company, and the same applies with the other organizations.
The reason for that is to make sure that we keep a separate way of handling each of the separate and distinct pillars of financial intermediation.
My friend has some idea that he can reverse that, that he could have everybody doing everybody's work but the ownership separate. We have discussed this for a long time. I am sure the House will realize that from what my friend had to say in debate. The issue has been well thought out, well debated over a long period of time.
I know my friend has been reading letters from very important and valued constituents in Mississauga. I guess the organizations that he and others belong to have had a number of conferences and a number of meetings and have gone over and discussed this. People involved in consumer affairs have gone through this issue. This has been a matter that has been worked out over a long period of time. Indeed it was the original suggestion of the finance committee in our 1985 report that the ownership be the way it is in the thrust of these bills but that strong walls be there to prevent intermingling of activity without the licence to do it.
We have a situation here which we have had for some considerable period of time. We want to continue with the situation that trust companies will not use their offices to sell or deal or advise on insurance. If a trust company wants to be involved in insurance or be related to an insurance company then it can cause to be incorporated a company or buy a company and have a separate company for the insurance operation.
The same applies with respect to trust operations and the like. If it is desirable to have some of the same personnel involved, that is a question of licensing per-
Govemment Orders
sonnel, but the offices have to be kept separate and the businesses policed separately.
The effect of what we want to see happen is the way these bills are organized. We believe that is in the best interest of the public generally. There may be argument, and my friend has presented his argument and there are people who would support my friend's argument, but the vast preponderance of people involved who know anything about this matter of intermediation and people concerned about the public interest accept and believe the way it is being proposed in these bills is the way that we ought to go.
It is with great regret, I must say, that we cannot at all support these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, on Motion No. 58 regarding the amendment that a trust should be able to act as an agent, this amendment was already dealt with in the finance committee and it was defeated. I do not see any reason for this amendment. We do not believe that trust companies should be able to sell all types of insurance.
The current trust legislation allow trusts to act as an agent for their customers in certain insurance transactions. For example, if you are going on a trip and you want travel insurance, you can go into your trust company and get it; the trust company can act as an agent. The finance department is on record as saying that trusts will be able to continue to do this under Bill C-4. Therefore, I do not see any reason for that amendment and we will be voting against it.
With regard to Motion No. 60, respecting the passage of information to insurance companies with the customer's consent, here again I am speaking against this amendment. We do not believe that trust companies should be able to sell all types of insurance. This would violate that ban. What would happen is that banks with their massive data bases would pass on to insurance companies huge lists of their customers that they could then use for target marketing. While a qualified insurance representative would be making the sale, the enormous resources the bank would have could easily lead to unequal competition and major disruptions in the industry.

For those reasons we will be voting against these amendments.

Motion No. 68.
That Bill C-4 be amended by adding immediately after line 16 at page 227 the following new clause:
"444. (1) A company must use plain language in all contracts related to financial services, applications for financial services and related documents which it provides to its customers who are natural persons.
(2)	Subsection (1) does not apply to words or forms of documents that are prescribed by law.
(3)	Subsection (2) does not apply to contracts, applications for financial services and related documents where the price of the financial service or the total liability assumed or to be assumed by the customer exceeds two hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
(4)	Proof that reasonable efforts have been made by the company to comply and maintain compliance with subsection (1) is a complete defence (a) in a prosecution under subsection (1), or (b) in a dispute about whether subsection (1) has been complied with.
(5)	The failure of a company to comply with subsection (1) does not affect the enforceability of any document referred to therein and may not be asserted by a customer or a company as a defence in an action or proceeding based on a document referred to in subsection (1).
(6)	As used in this section "customer" includes a natural person who is a guarantor or provides security to a company.
(7)	Subsections (1), (2), (3), (4), (5) and (6) shall come into force on the day which is two years after the coming into force of section 1 of this Act."
-Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to propose this amendment which is an amendment entitled "plain language". It requires trust companies to put into plain language various documents used by customers.
I am sure that from time to time you probably have had the experience where you looked at a document of a trust company and found that not only is it very difficult to read because it is in very fine print but also it has a lot of legal terminology.

November 26, 1991

I am proposing this amendment because I feel it is important that customers are able to read a document and understand what it is. Therefore it focuses on the needs of the reader or the consumer. It involves using short sentences and everyday words and would make the document easy to follow.
I do not think that customers should have to receive applications and contracts that are difficult to follow and difficult to understand exactly what is contained in them.
I want to acknowledge that some progress has been made in this regard with some financial institutions. I certainly thank them for that. But there is a lot more that needs to be done and the industry will acknowledge this. I have put before us this morning a "plain language" amendment which is legislation that is in several states of the United States at the moment. New York first introduced it in 1978 and I believe there are at least 10 states at the moment that have enacted plain language statutes.
Here in Canada the only province that has plain language legislation is Alberta which passed this in 1990.
In looking at the New York model, the results of this amendment are reported to be impressive. Experts there argue that a legal requirement for plain language is needed and that one just cannot leave this up to the voluntary initiatives. As I stated earlier the trend has been started in Canada. Some financial institutions have started putting their forms in plain language and readable language that the average customer can understand. But experts indicate that if this is really going to be accomplished right straight through it needs to be put into legislation. That is why I am moving this amendment.
I believe it is a reasonable amendment. It gives the financial institutions two years to get their documents into plain language. Furthermore, they are only required to do so with small customers such as those who borrow less than $250,000.
I think this is an amendment which certainly will be very beneficial for consumers using the services of trust companies. I would urge the House to support it.

Mr. Speaker, I very much appreciate the thrust of the member's concern. I have always felt that a great deal of our legislation is far too complicated for the ordinary person to read. The same of course applies to contracts in some cases. But the trouble is how to define "plain language".
Government Orders
If one could define plain language we would be all set. I suppose that would be either English or French plain language. The trouble is that what is plain to me may be exceptionally complicated to you. We have a difficulty right at the outset understanding what is plain language.
I suppose to put that spirit of making things readable and easily understandable and so on in legislation itself becomes exceptionally difficult. How can you legislate and say that this language is not plain but that language is plain? What is a plain linguistic operation?
I do not know. I am afraid I have got to say that while I very much appreciate the spirit of the amendment it is not an amendment that we can support because we just do not have any mechanism to adjudicate the issue of whether the language is plain or whether the language is convoluted.
I do not suppose that would be easy to do. For example, would we be faced with a situation on a contract of insurance or a contract of deposit that is required as a result of long studies in English law and court case after court case in determining what is really required? We could have a judge say: "The contract is set aside because in my view this particular contract is not plain enough".
Issues like time of the essence clauses that are required have a long history of litigation behind them. Notice clauses have a long history of litigation behind them.
I very much respect my friend's intention but I must say that the damage that she is trying to cure is going to create more damage in the cure than the cure proposed.
I believe what we have to do is rely on the industries that are in the business of marketing their product to market something that people can read. A number of institutions are doing that. They are being very careful how they lay it out to people they propose to deal with. They are doing that because they want to be able to say: "You can take a look at our contract and anybody can read it".
I think we ought to leave it at that. I believe we would only create litigation, controversy and problems if we were to support this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, I want to support my colleague from Prince Edward Island on the plain language suggestion. I do not believe that it is as difficult as my hon. friend from Mississauga says to put contracts into plain language. Plain language means very simply that it is language that can be understood by

November 26, 1991
Government Orders
a person who is reasonably intelligent and can read and write.
It has been known for a long time or it has been suspected at least for a long time by many people that contracts are made deliberately difficult in order to bamboozle rather than to enlighten. It is not beyond the realm of linguists to devise a plain language contract. The sooner that happens the better it will be in my opinion both for the industries and for individuals.
In this day and age there can be no rational argument not to put contracts and other legal niceties into plain and simple clear language. I am sure that that will pertain in both of the official languages of this country.
I say let us get on with doing that as soon as possible without any further delays and the kind of logic that my friend has brought in to this debate.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I only want to take a moment to speak on this particular issue.
I do agree with my hon. colleague from Mississauga that it is not always easy to define what plain language is. However, some things are obvious. I will just give you an example that derives from our own practices here in this House. Have you ever tried to explain to a constituent why our petition forms are preambled the way they are? I have presented petition forms to constituents who sent me back a blast in a letter asking me who did I think I was using language like that to make sure they did not understand. We ask the House of Commons to "humbly sheweth". How many people in this world would know what "humbly sheweth" is or what it does?
It means to shoe a horse.

speakerposition: Deputy House Leader of the Official Opposition; Liberal Party Deputy House Leader
speechtext:
Obviously it is well intentioned but we do not use Shakespearian English today in this House, nor elsewhere generally in society. The language has gradually evolved into something else.
I have come to the conclusion that some of the language utilized in some insurance contracts has not evolved along with the rest of the language. It is about time we modified that. My colleague from Malpeque has indicated previously that other jurisdictions have done it, so it is not a matter of us re-inventing the wheel. Other jurisdictions have done it. Maybe in some jurisdictions some elements have not worked. That is possible but we
have their experience to draw from. There are some 10 jurisdictions that operate in the system which at least to a degree resembles our forms at least in administration of justice.
If other liberal democracies have utilized a simpler form of language in order to at least tiy to make these documents understandable by some people who cannot understand them now, then we have achieved something.
I agree that some documents are harder to read than others. That is obvious.

Just think of how Le Devoir is written, for instance. It is well-known but not quite as easy to understand as other newspapers.
The same thing happens with legislation when we adopt a style of writing that can be much more complex than usual, and sometimes for no reason. We could make an effort to try and use, if at all possible, words that are a bit easier to understand than those we find in the existing legislation.

I had an occasion about a year ago of reading my automobile insurance policy. It is a shame that I did not think to bring it here this morning and read excerpts from it. It is not entirely clear to me that it is even the English language that is utilized in it. It sounds remotely similar but not very close. It is something entirely different to what we are used to listening to as a language in everyday English.

Presumably the wording of the French version is equally hard to understand.

I think our colleague has given us something to think about very seriously and we should consider it favourably. Plain language is not as easy to define as it could be but most people recognize gobbledegook when they see it.

speakeroldname: Mr. John R. Rodriguez (Nickel Belt) moved:
speechtext:
Motion No. 78.
That Bill C-4 be amended by adding immediately after line 19 at page 244 the following new clause:
"460. Notwithstanding anything in sections 453 to 459, no company may acquire or increase a substantial investment in a body corporate
(a)	if the body corporate is an insurance company to which Parts I to VII of the Canadian and British Insurance Companies Act apply or an insurance corporation incorporated by or under an Act of the legislature of a province; or
(b)	if the activities of the body corporate are substantially similar to those of a body corporate described in paragraph (a)."
He said: Mr. Speaker, earlier I said that it was the thinking of this party that in the financial institution structure, each institution ought to do the things for which it has received the patent, or licence.
Banks are to deal with things that relate to banking, insurance companies with things that are related to insurance companies, trust and loans with things that are related to trust and loan companies. We believe that the pillar structure has served the financial institutions of this country very well. Banks have grown in Canada, trust and loan companies have grown and insurance companies have grown. As a matter of fact, there has not been an insurance company in Canada that has gone broke since insurance companies came into being, largely because we had a pillar structure and we regulated the pillars.
I understand things have changed. I understand that there are a lot of cross pillar synergies going on. We now have to deal with this new reality where in fact they are doing each other's business so to speak, running around the ends of the pillars. We have no objection to banks entering into joint venture arrangements with insurance companies. They do it with creditor insurance for exam-
Government Orders
pie. When you take out a loan the loan is insured. The bank does not insure the loan, but it has entered the joint venture with x insurance company that insures the loan. Mortgage insurance is similar where a joint venture is entered into with an insurance company to insure mortgages.
It seems to me that we have no problem with those joint ventures, those kinds of networking arrangements which are disclosed and regulated. That is the whole principle of the question of banks marketing insurance.
This particular amendment would prohibit a trust and loan company from owning an insurance company. I tell you that we have thrown up the spectre of what is going to happen when they start buying each other. In fact if you look at the market right now, the smaller trust companies are recognizing that they cannot survive with this upcoming legislation. Many of them are now looking for a bed fellow. Many of them are looking for a partner.
I want to tell you that you are going to see a period of merging going on that will make your head spin. At the end of the day, when it is all done, you are going to end up with the super financial institution. It will have subsidiaries but it will all be one super pocket. When that happens, we will have a concentration of economic power the likes of which we have never seen in this country.
This amendment is one of the ways we want to put the animals back in their cages. It attempts to do that.
I have heard the hon. member for Mississauga South say insurance companies should do insurance, banks should do banking. In fact, I want him to explain to me how it is that an insurance company can sell such financial instruments as RRSPs and GICs and what does an annuity have to do with insurance. It is a financial arrangement once you hit the magic 90 that you are going to live forever. What is so magic about that? Why is that not an instrument that a bank can sell? It does not make any sense to me.
What makes sense is recognizing a joint venture arrangement. That makes a lot more sense than forcing financial institutions to go out and either buy an insurance company, if they want to get involved in the full ramifications of what this legislation will provide, or else start one.

November 26, 1991
Government Orders
It does not seem to make any sense because that is going to be very costly in the long run. Only the large and powerful institutions will be able to do that in any event.
This amendment is in keeping with the philosophy that we have expressed throughout. The pillar system has built a very sound financial institution structure in this country. It has served Canadians very well. In some mad dash to deregulate, we will end up throwing out the baby with the bath water.
I warn the danger inherent is that you are going to have a meltdown. One morning you are going to wake up and find just as the Californians did, that there are really only two banks in all of California and now one is buying the other, so there will be only one bank in California, just one.
We see the deregulation in the United States and what it is doing to financial institutions there. What is happening is a meltdown in the United States. They are buying out each other. They are bailing each other out. They are going to have large humungous institutions.
I ask the members of the House to consider positively this amendment. I think it will make sure that the pillar system remains, but will allow the joint venturing and networking which we have no problem with.

This amendment is an attempt to turn the clock back, and the clock is not going to go back very easily. There are 20 insurance companies and trust companies already sharing ownership. To all of a sudden go with this amendment and prohibit the acquisition of one by the other would not wash with the realities of today.
The fact is that we are keeping the pillars of intermediation separate. In the thrust of all of the bills, we are allowing one institution to acquire another institution or be related to it in cross-ownership, but again operating separately.
I understand my friend's philosophy, but it is not the philosophy of the legislation. It is not the philosophy that has generally been accepted by people in all branches of the intermediation industry. I understand my friend's wanting to establish a new order, but the new order is not one that is acceptable to anyone in the financial industries, or to very many people in the financial industries anyway. The consequence is that we cannot accept my friend's decision to try to rewrite the way things are going.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Mississauga South has mentioned presently in Canada at least 20 insurance companies now own a trust company or are part of a conglomerate that owns a trust company. In view of that it only seems logical that trusts should be able to own insurance companies.
We hear concerns expressed about corporate concentration, and certainly that is a concern that I have. But there are two ways that would be dealt with. First, there is the Competition Act, which applies to any questionable acquisitions and second, there is the Minister of Finance. He can refuse a merger that would not serve the best interests of the Canadian financial system.
Another fact I would like to point out is that six out of the top 10 large Canadian insurance companies are takeover-proof. What I mean by that is that they are mutuals. They are owned by the policyholders and, therefore, cannot be taken over.
Finally, the Conference Board of Canada told the finance committee when we were reviewing the financial institution legislation that it sees no competition problems if trusts are given the power to buy insurance companies.
For those reasons we will be voting against this amendment.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me that the debate on this amendment, if I understand it correctly, illustrates the difference between the two basic approaches being taken here by the government and by the NDP. The government seeks to maintain the appearances of the four pillar system on which our financial industry has been based over the years whereas we are seeking to maintain the reality of that pillar system.
Having said that, it seems to me that what we have here with this-as the hon. member for Nickel Belt called it- mad rush to deregulate is really a mad rush to imitate. It is a mad rush to mimic what we see going on south of the border which is so very, very symptomatic of other things that we have seen. With respect to this issue I would say as I might say with respect to others: What is the origin and the locus of this self hate for Canada and Canadian institutions and the Canadian way of doing things that we find on the other side of the House? What has happened? I did not realize that I grew up in such a bad country with all these things that needed to be
November 26, 1991

changed: the way we ran our transport system, the way we ran our health care system and you name it. I had no idea that I lived in such an abominable society, that it needed to be so radically altered and so radically Americanized.
That is what is going on. We see here a kind of self loathing on the part of the government that everything Canadian has to be mutated and altered and made more like the Americans in some way or another. This is pathological. This is a deep, deep psycho-political sickness on the part of the government and it reaches into everything. Everything is being touched by this sickness of having to imitate. Let us get rid of anything that is Canadian, anything that worked and that made, in this case, for a very sound financial system, one of the soundest in the world. My God, it is an embarrassment. There may be people or institutions that cannot make all the money they want to make and this reduces our self image. We are not a place where people can be real greedy guts, they can only be half greedy guts so, let us change it.
I just do not understand it and I find this whole mess the government is entering into here to be just another symptom of this malaise that unfortunately affects the whole country. If the Conservatives just want to bring themselves down it would not be so bad, but they are taking a very good country with them.

Mr. Speaker, I also would like to intervene in the debate. The amendment that is being proposed by my colleague from Nickel Belt would prohibit trust companies from acquiring insurance companies.
This is part of our whole general thrust in opposing the government's resolutions and motions that would radically alter and change our financial institutions.
Yesterday, when I spoke on some of the other amendments I brought up the question of public interest. My friend from Mississauga South talked about the interest of the insurance companies and the trust companies, but he really did not explain how this would be in the public interest.

They do not seem to care about this.
Government Orders

The concern I have as this government moves along in this legislation, and my colleague from Nickel Belt yesterday put into the record, is with the comment made by the former chairman of the finance committee during hearings of the finance committee, that this was a cut deal. I asked where was the public interest when the insurance companies and the banks and the life insurance companies and so forth sat down and worked out this deal.
It is up the government to protect the public interest. It is up to the government to demonstrate, when it moves legislation through this House that the public will benefit, that the public will be protected. Yet as we hear government spokesmen defending this legislation, not once have I heard them attempt to justify anything on the basis of public interest. They are here representing the interests of the insurance companies, the trusts and the banks, but their job is to protect the interest of the public and they are not doing that. They are protecting the interests of the banks and the trusts and so forth, but not the public. They are not doing their job. They are negligent in fulfilling their job of protecting the public interest.
Is it in the public's interest to have the few large financial institutions that take deposits and so forth to own trusts and insurance? Is it in the public's interest to see the money they deposit in institutions being used somehow to acquire insurance companies, to be used to expand the commercial and other financial interests of this trust or bank, whatever the case may be?
It is the government's job to ensure that when people put their money into a deposit that the banks will do everything in their power to act in the best interest of those depositors and make certain that their deposits are not put at risk.
Now we have a situation where these deposit institutions can acquire other commercial ventures, other financial ventures. They might take the depositors' money and put that at risk for the sake of the financial interest of the commercial enterprise or the financial enterprise.
That is wrong. It will shake the trust people have in the deposit taking institutions. That will occur because we have the misfortune of having a government that did not act first and foremost to protect the public interest.

Government Orders
With this particular amendment, I have not heard any justification from the government for allowing trust companies to own life insurance companies from the point of view of how this will serve the public interest. Therefore I cannot support the government's thrust and will support the amendments introduced by my colleague from Nickel Belt south.

The first one of these is Motion No. 1 which deals with the prohibition against the federal Crown establishing a bank.
I do not know what it is that motivates a government to apply what I consider to be medieval thinking to the state. Why does the government want to exclude the Crown from establishing a federal bank or a commercial bank? Why would we close the door to that option at this particular point?
Now we are embarking on deregulation of financial institutions. It is a deregulation of the financial institutions and we just do not know where this road is leading. The federal government in the past has established the FBDB as was pointed out by one of my colleagues yesterday and it has established the Bank of Canada. Yet here we have a prohibition against establishing a commercial bank. I just do not understand this medieval view which I have seen from time to time being expressed that somehow or other the state ought to exclude itself from having a bank.
We all are saying that we want to go into Europe and compete with the Europeans. We say Europe 92 is the way to go. Yet if you look at the European experience governments in Europe are right up to their armpits in commercial banking.
France is very involved in its commercial banking. The Germans are involved in their banking system. In this country we not only do not get involved in it we now turn around and bring in a law that says we cannot at all. We cannot have a bank.
I know our party has long held a policy that we wanted to nationalize a bank. I have serious doubts about that. I think that has probably been put on the back burner because who wants to go out and spend billions of dollars of the taxpayers' money buying one.
It seems to me that if we are going to get into the banking business the way to go is to start your own. That option is not at all open to us when this passes. Imagine a government that has such a jaundiced view of its own role and its own function that it would forbid itself the option of at some point maybe needing to have a window on the banking industry. By God when these bills pass this is going to be a different animal. The financial
Government Orders
institutions of this country are going to be a different breed all together.
I once described them as animals. I gave them animal names in the form of a fable. I had them in their cages. The problem is somebody is opening up these cages.
Already the Royal Bank has got the lion as its symbol. It has got the globe and it is hugging the globe to its chest. That is very symbolic of where they are headed. That is the first thing. My amendment would give to the Crown and keep the option open to the Crown to establish a bank.
Second, I have the two other amendments namely Motions Nos. 4 and 5. No. 5 is consequential on No. 4. Basically Motions Nos. 4 and 5 look to what is happening with this legislation.
When we held hearings into the Bank Act and the Trust and Loans Act we found that Canada Trust for one is as big as the smallest of the five banks. Canada Trust says: "We would love to become a bank. We are growing. We would not mind becoming a bank". There is only one problem wrong with that. Canada Trust is owned by somebody else so the 10 per cent rule could not be applied to it.
My Motions Nos. 4 and 5 recognize that after this legislation gets passed some of these financial institutions are going to grow. It is quite possible that you can have a very large trust and loan company. It would be very large in actual size and yet the ownership could be closely held.
What we have said in this motion is to have a sliding scale of ownership. If you grow beyond a certain size then the way you protect the shareholders and investors is to have the wide ownership provision. This is the 10 per cent wide ownership provision that is applying to banks at the moment. They can decide. The larger you get the more widely held the ownership has to be. So the institution has options. It seems to me that sliding scale is a protection for depositors and it is a protection for investors and a protection for all Canadians because when they fail it is the taxpayers who pick up the tab. Let us not kid ourselves. The CDIC picks up the buck.
I know that colleagues yesterday mentioned Standard Trust. In that episode the taxpayers picked up roughly about $250 million. That came right out of the taxpayers' pockets. There was a closely held company and a small

financial institution. But imagine now, given this legislation. It is a licence to grow big. The dangers are going to be there.
My Liberal and Tory colleagues got together to reduce the auditors to one. In a new sphere and in a new era we are going to have larger financial institutions. At the same time we are removing or not permitting the kinds of built-in controls such as the widely-held ownership control for larger financial institutions. I think it is a big mistake to dismiss the idea of two auditors given the size to which these financial institutions can now grow. They can grow and become sumo wrestlers as I have said time and time again in the past. They can represent Canada in global competition. I know that is where the Liberal Party is moving these days to join the Conservatives in this mad dash to get bigger and bigger and bigger and bigger. At the same time the well thought out sliding scale of the green paper in 1985 has been thrown out.
I know that the member for Mississauga South will say that is not in the cards because the financial institutions will not accept it. I want to remind members again that it is not the financial institutions which will decide what is best for Canada. Parliament decides that. It is the legislators of this country who decide what is best for Canada not a couple of overfed bankers and bagmen and bandits meeting in some room on Bay Street or on Bank Street deciding it. It is legislators who decide that. I am sorry the member for Mississauga South has broken with his past.

Mr. Speaker, it is always entertaining to hear from my friend from Nickel Belt.
We have two amendments and the first amendment is in connection with governments incorporating commercially under this particular statute.
My friend will know that it has not been the policy of the Government of Canada under any government to allow a provincial government to incorporate a chartered bank and that prohibition remains in the Bank Act.
The federal government, if it wants to start doing something of that nature, would incorporate a bank by statute much the same as the federal government incorporated the Federal Business Development Bank and the Bank of Canada.
This bill is designed to handle the affairs of commercial banks.
Dealing with the scaled ownership amendments, Motions Nos. 4 and 5, my friend will know that all of the Schedule A banks in this country must be widely held in that no person or group of persons acting in concert can hold more than 10 per cent of the voting stock. That is the way we intend to keep it.
With respect to trust companies and Schedule B banks-we have a number of Schedule B banks in this country, and my friend will know that they are all foreign owned-they are now subject to the control limitations of $750 million in paid-in capital. If they exceed $750 million in paid-in capital they must subscribe to the rule that makes them divest up to 35 per cent of their ownership to Canadians in a widely held fashion.
I think my friend should accept that because it is a very important move in terms of making sure that those who come to this country to do banking operate in the same fashion as Canadians operate in this country. So Schedule B banks are required under the legislation, if they reach $750 million in paid-in capital, to start making their shares available in the marketplace to the extent of 35 per cent.
The sliding scale was well debated over a five year period. It was found on examination to be unacceptable at this time. I had something to do with making the suggestion of the sliding scale when I was chairman of the finance committee back in 1985, but the matter has been handled over a period of time. We have looked at this matter very carefully to see how we best could, as my friend said, protect the interests of the public and protect the interests of the nation. This particular format that we now have is viewed by everyone in the industries and by the government and respecting the interests of the individual as the best way we can proceed at this time.
I want to say to my friend with regard to the whole question of the Canada Trusts and the Royal Trusts of this world being narrowly controlled, massive organizations, that the act prevents them from becoming banks unless they become widely held. Perhaps that is as it should be. Canada Trust can, if it wants to, become widely held and become a bank. But unless it becomes widely held, it is the view at this stage that banks not be narrowly held in Canada. Once foreign banks pass $750 million in paid-in capital, they too must have market participation. We believe that this is the best framework at this time in terms of the ownership issue. The
November 26, 1991

ownership issue has been debated and debated at great length and we believe that this is the best arrangement that can be arrived at today.

Mr. Speaker, with regard to Motion No. 1, which would give the government the power to own a bank, as I indicated yesterday we studied the whole financial institution legislation for over a year and we heard over 100 witnesses and never did we have a provincial government come and request this power.
Never did we have an individual or consumer group come before the finance committee and request that provincial governments be given the power to incorporate a bank.
As a result, this issue has not been studied by the committee and furthermore, a government which wishes to own a financial institution can do so by owning a provincial trust company, as has been done in Ontario and Alberta. For these reasons, we will be voting against that amendment.
With regard to Motions Nos. 4 and 5, this amendment would subject foreign Schedule 2 banks to a sliding scale in ownership. In other words, the larger the foreign bank the more widely it would have to be held.
The current Bank Act, as indicated by the hon. member from Mississauga, says that a foreign Schedule 2 may be closely held indefinitely unless it surpasses $750 million in capital through the acquisition of a Canadian financial institution. In that case it would be required to have 35 per cent of its shares in public ownership.
In Canada, trust and insurance companies will only have to meet that 35 per cent rule as opposed to the sliding scale that has been suggested. We see no reason whatsoever that foreign Schedule 2 banks should be treated any differently.
The current Bank Act allows foreign Schedule 2 banks to be closely held indefinitely. Certainly we have heard no evidence at the finance committee to make a spiel that there should be a change in this policy.
We will be voting against these amendments.

Mr. Speaker, the amendments being proposed today would allow the federal government to get into the commercial
Government Orders
banking business. We have heard some spokespeople from the Liberal and the Conservative parties argue against that amendment.
It is not that we envisage in this amendment that the government would go off and nationalize a bank. I do not think that would make any sense. Certainly there might be occasions from time to time when this might make some sense, as in the earlier part of the last decade when we had the Canadian Commercial Bank and the Northland Bank going under.
It took a lot of the taxpayers' money to bail out the depositors through subsidization of the deposit insurance. Many of the depositors, especially in the Canadian Commercial Bank, were the banks because the Canadian Commercial Bank was offering quite an attractive interest rate on short term money.
Here we had the quite interesting situation where the government borrows money from the banks and pays interest on it and it is part of our deficit. Here we have the Canadian government borrowing money from the banks in order to pay the banks some moneys they would have lost with the collapse of the Canadian Commercial Bank.
I see our former chairman scratching his head and smiling. He knows that this was one of the ridiculous moments in Canadian high finance. We saved our great free enterprisers who took the risk in order to get a few basic points higher than interest rates. Surely they knew that the Canadian Commercial Bank was offering slightly higher interest rates which it needed to attract deposits. It was having problems. They knew they would eventually be able to get any money they were going to lose back from the Canadian government. It seemed to me at that moment that rather than the Canadian government using taxpayers' money to help save the depositors of those financial institutions, the Canadian government should have just taken them over and continued to operate them as commercial banks. It would have saved the Canadian public a lot of money. It would have saved some depositors some money. It certainly would have saved the Deposit Insurance Corporation money and it made sense. At that point it would have made sense if the Canadian government had taken over those two failing institutions and continued to operate them.

November 26, 1991

Very often when a bank goes under it is because it had too many loans out in terms of real estate and the oil industry. This was the particular problem both with the Northland and the Canadian Commercial Banks. We also know that these are cyclical things. If we had been able to continue operating those financial institutions over a decade, some of the bad loans for mortgages on real estate that had declined in value would have been recovered as the value of that real estate went back up again.
I maintain that would have been an ideal opportunity for the government to acquire those institutions and continue to operate them. However, the legislation prohibits the government from doing that. If the government really wants to, it can go back and change the legislation, therefore why have it in the act in the first place?
It is not very often that we see something being legislated telling us what the government cannot do. In terms of the workings of this House it does not make sense. It is inappropriate to have in the act a statement saying that the government cannot do something. One begins to wonder why the government insists that it wants this in. I suspect it is trying to please other folks by giving another line of defence in case the government comes to a situation where it actually wants to operate a commercial bank. It would mean that the government would first have to bring that legislation to the House and amend it before proceeding to act on acquiring and setting up a commercial bank. It is an odd piece of legislation in the act and should not be there.
The other amendment that I think is important is the sliding scale. It originated from the former minister for financial institutions when she presented her green paper. Basically, it makes sense that trust companies which want to deal like banks are acquiring a lot of the powers of banks with this legislation. They will be able to do things that banks do. I agree with the bankers that "if it smells like a bank, if it walks like a bank and talks like a bank, then by golly, it becomes a bank". This is the situation we will arrive at in terms of the trust. So why not take it all the way and require some rules and regulations in terms of their ownership?
What the amendment proposes I think is quite modest. It proposes that a trust can be 100 per cent owned if it has assets of less than $10 billion. It has to divest part of its ownership if it has assets of no more than $20 billion. In other words if it has assets of $20 billion, no one individual or entity controlled by an individual can own more than 75 per cent of that trust.
With reference to the sliding scale, the third step is that no individual or entity controlled by an individual can own more than 50 per cent if the total assets reach $30 billion. No individual can own or control a trust for more than 25 per cent if the total assets are up to $40 billion. If it is over $40 billion what we require through this amendment is that no individual can control more than 10 per cent.
Those are not outrageous numbers. These are huge amounts of assets, wealth and power. Is it in the public interest to have so much power being concentrated in the hands of one individual?
It is not just us New Democrats making this point in this House even though we are a lonely voice here. A well respected international magazine The Economist had a November 9, 1991 article entitled "Canadian finance: Untrustworthy?" I wish to put on the record this quote:
The banks have long argued that allowing an industrial or commercial concern to control a financial institution is a recipe for disaster and mismanagement. The authorities in Ottawa have resisted their call to impose on trusts the wide ownership rules that apply to banks themselves. More trust company failures could prompt the government to think again.
One hopes and one wonders at what point will the government start thinking again.
We have seen during the eighties a number of trust companies going under. I think of Pioneer Trust in Regina. The workings, the management and the ownership of Pioneer Trust at the time I do not think should be held up as an ideal model. There were some questionable "business decisions". There were some suggestions of conflict of interest in there between the commercial interest of some of the directors and owners of that particular trust and the businesses that the trust was involved in, the type of loans it gave and the type of assets it looked at in terms of securing loans.
Imagine if Pioneer Trust had been a $10 billion or a $40 billion institution and the same type of mentality was occurring. Think of the the tremendous disaster it would
November 26, 1991

have created and the economic harm it would have done to Canada and to the depositors.
This amendment is about some form of protection to ensure that one or two individuals do not control so much power and assets that their wrongdoings can create a tremendous public harm to the country.

"215. He said: Mr. Speaker, do you remember yesterday when we were dealing with Bill C-4, the trust companies act, that we moved the exact same amendment?
The purpose of the amendment is to require disclosure and shareholder approval of the remuneration of the five highest paid directors, officers or employees of a bank. As I said yesterday, this is simply an extension of the democracy that we support in the political operations of
November 26, 1991

our country. In a way, a bank or a company is much like a country.
In a country the electors, the people of the country are really the shareholders. The assets of those shareholders are managed by the people whom they elect. That is government and that is Parliament.
All the people who are shareholders in this democracy of Canada know or have available to them what are the wages of their directors, their chief officers, the cabinet and members of Parliament. Their wages are available to the public because the public who are the shareholders are paying the loan. They are paying the freight.
They have a right to know. They have a right to know in the same way in a bank the shareholders and potential investors have a right to know. After a while, that money is coming out of potential dividends and it is going to pay the salaries of the top officers.
Can you imagine the scene now where the shareholders can vote the wages of the board of directors of the company, which is really peanuts compared to what the chief operating officials of the bank get? Yet the shareholders are not asked to vote and to approve the wages of the top officials of the bank. I think there is a need for that kind of transparency because there is what is called accountability. Where there is transparency, there is accountability.
This is not just simply some sort of titillating desire to be pornographic about the earnings of bankers. That is not what it is all about. In fact, in the United States this information is all filed with their securities commission.
What we are asking here is not something radical. In fact, we have had the experience. Imagine that when we wanted to find out what the chief officials of corporations earn, we have to actually go to the United States and access the information there.
We used to collect this under the old Corporations and Labour Unions Returns Act. CALURA we called it. Do you remember CALURA? When this government came into office, it scrapped that.
There was an opportunity at one time under CALURA when we could go and look up this information. We cannot do that now. We have to go south of the border. We have to depend on the American process getting information for us. That does not seem to me to be fair ball.

In fact, the Ontario Security Commission is seized of this matter at the moment as we speak. They are attempting to decide whether they should require this information to be filed.
We are asking the government to recognize that it has a leadership role here and it has control over banks and financial institutions because of Bill C-19 and the Bank Act. We should be leading the way. We should be providing the opportunity for the shareholders and the potential investors of banks to get this information, information which they, on their own, are not able to obtain even from their own institutions of which they have a share. I appeal to the members in the House. I appeal to my colleague from Mississauga South who, from time to time, displays a sense of fair play. I know he is always concerned about the interests of the shareholders. Here is an opportunity to put something into the bill.
Good heavens, it is not radical, it is not something that is not done by our major trading partner. To hear the bankers tell it and to hear the government tell it, that is supposedly one of the spin-offs from the free trade agreement. After all, we are allowing American banks to come in here under the agreement and we treat them as if they are Canadians.
It has been shown by no less a person than Doug Peters that in fact we do not have the same reciprocal access to the American markets in banking and financial institutions as they have here. If it were working the way the government envisaged it working and the way I see all the Canadian banks running down into the United States, why would they? If they are going into the United States as they are, they are going to have to comply with American rules and they will have to reveal the information down there. So what is this nonsense that we cannot lead. It is not a question of leading, it is a question of what is logical. We are into a free trade agreement where you have a level playing field.
It seems to me to be logical that the government would want to put in its bank legislation the same kind of rules that apply to bankers in our chief trading partner. I do not see a problem with this. I really do not.
Look at the things that we are interested in having put on the record.
